title: An essential convex hull criterion for false confidence in location models
shortTitle: Which false hypotheses can a probability favour? A convex hull answer
oneLine: In location models with light-tailed errors, a hypothesis is calibrated at every threshold at a parameter exactly when that parameter is not strictly inside its essential convex hull, and a finite test warns of high confidence in a false hypothesis.
abstract: Operators compute a probability of collision, and with large uncertainty it is small even if a collision is certain. Balch, Martin and Ferson (2019) named this false confidence and proved that affected hypotheses exist; Martin (2024) asked which. This candidate answers exactly for flat-prior posteriors in location models with radially decreasing errors. For exponential-power errors with p > 1, a hypothesis is valid at every threshold at a parameter exactly when that parameter lies outside the interior of the closed convex hull of the essential support of the hypothesis. The equivalence holds for a radial density g with tail probability S if and only if liminf S(R)/g(R − b) = 0 for every b > 0; tails like exp(−r log r) satisfy this in dimension one and fail in every higher dimension. Only almost-halfspaces are calibrated from both sides, which corrects a conjecture of Martin (2024) in these models, since a ball is not affected, and only strictly monotone functions of one linear form have exact marginal posteriors. With log-concave errors, if a closed convex set contains the complement of the hypothesis and has posterior mass at most s < 1/2 when the observation equals the truth, the hypothesis receives posterior probability at least 1 − s with sampling probability at least one half. The sufficient direction is elementary and halfspace validity is in Martin (2023). All-threshold failure may occur only at low thresholds. The model assumes known shape and exact matching. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Hull criterion (Theorem 1, proof): under the tail condition (T), a hypothesis is valid at every threshold at a parameter exactly when that parameter is outside the interior of its essential convex hull; (T) is also necessary.
Exact tail condition (Lemma 0, proof): exponential-power errors satisfy (T) exactly for p > 1; tails like exp(−r log r) satisfy it in dimension one and fail it in every higher dimension.
Two-sided classification (Theorem 4, Corollary 5, proof): four calibration regimes; only almost-halfspaces are calibrated from both sides, correcting a conjecture of Martin (2024) in these models.
Exact marginalisation (Theorem 6, proof): only strictly monotone functions of one linear form have exact marginal posteriors at every parameter.

High confidence (Theorem 8, proof and Table 2): with log-concave errors, Q_θ(C) ≤ s < 1/2 for a closed convex C containing the complement gives posterior probability at least 1 − s at least half the time; at σ/R = 10 a certain collision gives Pc ≤ 0.01 with probability one.

narration:
This is a short audio briefing on a new Evidence Press research candidate: an essential convex hull criterion for false confidence in location models.

Satellite operators compute the probability that two objects will collide. There is a catch. When uncertainty is large, that probability is small even if a collision is certain. In 2019, Balch, Martin and Ferson named this false confidence, and proved that some false hypotheses tend to look well supported. In 2024, Martin asked which ones.

This paper gives an exact answer for a standard class of models. Take the hypothesis, and draw the smallest convex shape around it, ignoring pieces of zero volume. With light-tailed errors, the hypothesis is calibrated at every threshold, at a given parameter value, exactly when that value is not strictly inside the shape. The paper also finds the exact tail condition for this to hold. It shows that only halfspaces are calibrated from both sides. That corrects Martin's conjecture that every non-linear hypothesis is affected, because a ball is not.

There is a practical result too. With log-concave errors, suppose everything outside a hypothesis fits in a convex set with small posterior mass, when the data land on the truth. Then the hypothesis gets high probability at least half the time. If the uncertainty is ten times the object size, a certain collision gives a computed probability of at most one percent, every time.

Some limits. The easy direction is elementary, and part of it appears in Martin's earlier work. Failure at every threshold may happen only at low thresholds, so the shape alone says nothing about ninety-five percent confidence. The model assumes a known shape and an exact match. The search for earlier work is not proof of priority.

The proofs are written out, and scripts check the worked numbers. Review was internal and AI-assisted, with no proof assistant. This remains an unrefereed candidate, released on 4 November 2026. The paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press page.

This briefing uses a synthetic voice, and it is not additional scientific evidence.
